title: API Design Fundamentals
summary: API design is the act of making decisions that will constrain and enable developers for years. Well-designed APIs are intuitive, consistent, evolvable, and secure. REST, GraphQL, gRPC, and WebSockets each excel in different contexts. Understanding the principles of resource modeling, error handling, versioning, and security transforms API design from guesswork into engineering.

sections.title: REST Principles and Resource Modeling
paragraphs: REST (Representational State Transfer) organizes APIs around resources (nouns) rather than actions (verbs). A resource is any entity your API exposes: /users, /orders, /products. HTTP verbs express operations: GET (read), POST (create), PUT/PATCH (update), DELETE (delete). The URL identifies the resource; the verb identifies the operation. This uniformity makes REST APIs predictable: a developer familiar with one REST API can intuit how another works without reading documentation.

Resource naming: use plural nouns for collections (/users), singular resource identifiers (/users/123), and nested resources for relationships (/users/123/orders). Avoid verbs in URLs (/users/123/activate is wrong; use PATCH /users/123 with body {status: 'active'} or POST /users/123/activations for the activation event). Hierarchical nesting should be limited to 2–3 levels; deeper nesting creates brittle URLs that change when relationships change.

HTTP status codes must be used semantically: 200 OK (success with body), 201 Created (new resource; include Location header), 204 No Content (success without body), 400 Bad Request (client error; validation failed), 401 Unauthorized (missing/invalid auth), 403 Forbidden (authenticated but not authorized), 404 Not Found, 422 Unprocessable Entity (valid syntax but semantic error), 429 Too Many Requests, 500 Internal Server Error. Never return 200 with an error body ('success: false')—HTTP status codes exist precisely to convey outcome without parsing the body.
bullets: Resources as nouns: /users, /orders, /products; HTTP verbs express operations
URL structure: /resources (collection), /resources/id (item), /resources/id/sub-resources
HTTP semantics: 200/201/204 success; 4xx client errors; 5xx server errors; use them correctly
Avoid verbs in URLs; use nouns + HTTP methods; use sub-resources for state transitions

sections.title: GraphQL: Query What You Need
paragraphs: GraphQL is a query language for APIs where clients specify exactly the data they need in a single request. Unlike REST where the server defines response shape, GraphQL clients define their own response shape. A mobile app needing only user name and avatar sends a query { user(id: 123) { name, avatar } } and receives exactly those fields. A desktop app needing full user details sends a richer query. This eliminates over-fetching (REST returning 50 fields when you need 3) and under-fetching (REST requiring 5 round trips to assemble a page).

GraphQL's type system is both its strength and its learning curve. All data is typed: scalars (String, Int, Boolean, ID), object types, enums, interfaces, and unions. The schema is the contract between client and server—once published, any breaking change (removing a field, changing a type) breaks all clients. Schema stitching and federation (Apollo Federation) allow splitting a large schema across multiple services while presenting a unified API to clients.

The N+1 problem is GraphQL's most common performance pitfall. A query for 100 users, each with their latest order, naively triggers 1 query for all users + 100 queries for each user's latest order = 101 queries. DataLoader (Facebook's batching library) solves this: instead of querying the database per-user, it collects all user IDs from a request's resolvers and fires one batched query for all of them. DataLoader is essential for any GraphQL API serving relational data.
bullets: GraphQL: clients specify exact shape; eliminates over-fetching and under-fetching
Type system: schema is the contract; breaking changes (remove field) break all clients
Apollo Federation: split schema across multiple services; unified API surface
DataLoader: batches N+1 queries within a request; essential for relational GraphQL data

sections.title: gRPC: High-Performance Service Communication
paragraphs: gRPC uses Protocol Buffers (Protobuf) as its interface definition language and binary serialization format. Protobuf serialization is 3–10x smaller and faster than JSON: a 10KB JSON payload becomes 1–3KB in Protobuf. gRPC uses HTTP/2, enabling request multiplexing (multiple in-flight requests on one connection), server push, and header compression. For internal microservice communication where latency and throughput matter, gRPC is significantly faster than REST+JSON.

Protobuf message definitions are strongly typed and versioned. Field numbers (not field names) identify fields in the wire format: field 1, field 2, etc. Adding new fields with new field numbers is backward compatible (old clients ignore unknown fields). Removing fields by reserving their field number is backward compatible (new clients handle missing fields). Never reuse field numbers—this causes deserialization corruption. This versioning discipline enables gRPC APIs to evolve without breaking existing clients.

gRPC supports four communication patterns: unary (single request, single response—like HTTP), server streaming (single request, stream of responses—for real-time data feeds), client streaming (stream of requests, single response—for file uploads), and bidirectional streaming (both sides stream simultaneously—for real-time collaboration, gaming). These patterns are natively supported by the gRPC framework; implementing server streaming in REST requires SSE or WebSockets with significant boilerplate.
bullets: Protobuf: 3–10x smaller and faster than JSON; strongly typed; backward-compatible via field numbers
HTTP/2: multiplexing + header compression; superior to HTTP/1.1 for many concurrent requests
Four patterns: unary, server streaming, client streaming, bidirectional streaming
Use for: internal microservice comms, high-throughput data pipelines, latency-sensitive services

sections.title: API Error Handling and Idempotency
paragraphs: Error responses must be consistent and informative. The standard: a JSON body with a machine-readable error code (string enum, not integer), a human-readable message, and optionally a details field for validation errors. Example: {error: {code: 'INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS', message: 'Account balance insufficient for this transfer', details: [{field: 'amount', issue: 'exceeds_balance'}]}}. The code field allows clients to handle specific errors programmatically; the message is for display. Never return 500 with generic 'Internal Server Error' messages—log the details server-side and return a unique error ID the client can reference in support tickets.

Idempotency keys transform non-idempotent operations (POST /charges) into safe-to-retry ones. The client generates a UUID and includes it as an Idempotency-Key header; the server stores the response keyed by this ID. If the same key is sent again (due to timeout/retry), the server returns the stored response without re-executing the operation. Stripe's implementation: idempotency keys are stored for 24 hours; requests with the same key within 24 hours return the cached response. Implement idempotency for all state-mutating endpoints that clients might retry.

Pagination is mandatory for list endpoints. Never return unbounded lists: response size is unpredictable, server and client memory usage is unbounded, and latency is uncontrollable. Offset/limit pagination (GET /users?offset=100&limit=20) is simple but breaks when items are inserted or deleted during pagination (items may be skipped or duplicated). Cursor-based pagination (GET /users?after=cursor123&limit=20) is stable: the cursor points to a specific item; insertions and deletions don't affect the page position. Use cursor-based pagination for user-facing paginated lists.
bullets: Error format: code (machine-readable enum) + message (human readable) + details (validation)
Idempotency key: UUID header; server caches response; safe to retry POST operations
Pagination: always paginate list endpoints; cursor-based > offset for stability
Return unique error_id for 500 errors; log details server-side; allow support ticket reference

sections.title: Authentication, Rate Limiting, and API Design Best Practices
paragraphs: API authentication: API keys for server-to-server integrations (simple, long-lived, easy to revoke per key); OAuth 2.0 + JWT for user-delegated access (user grants an application limited access to their data without sharing their password); mutual TLS (mTLS) for service-to-service internal APIs (each service has a certificate; cryptographic identity verification). Never put API keys in URLs (they appear in server logs, browser history); always in headers (Authorization: Bearer <token> or X-API-Key: <key>).

Rate limiting protects APIs from abuse and prevents individual clients from monopolizing resources. Common strategies: fixed window (count requests in a fixed 60-second window; reset at the window boundary—vulnerable to boundary bursts), sliding window (count requests in the most recent 60 seconds—more accurate but heavier), token bucket (clients accumulate tokens at a fixed rate; each request consumes a token; allows bursts up to bucket size). Use different limits for different tiers (free: 100 req/min; paid: 10K req/min) and different operations (write endpoints stricter than read). Return 429 with Retry-After header when rate limited.

API design checklist: (1) Consistent resource naming (plural nouns). (2) Correct HTTP status codes. (3) Idempotency for all mutating endpoints. (4) Cursor-based pagination for all lists. (5) Consistent error format. (6) Authentication on all non-public endpoints. (7) Rate limiting with 429 and Retry-After. (8) Versioning strategy (URL path /v1 or header Accept: application/vnd.api.v1+json). (9) OpenAPI/Swagger specification. (10) Deprecation notices before breaking changes.
bullets: Auth: API keys for server-to-server; OAuth 2.0 + JWT for user delegation; mTLS for service mesh
Rate limiting: token bucket (allows bursts); sliding window (accurate); per-tier limits
Return 429 + Retry-After on rate limit; don't silently drop requests
Checklist: nouns, status codes, idempotency, pagination, errors, auth, rate limits, versioning, OpenAPI

deepDive.title: API Versioning Strategies
paragraphs: URL versioning (/v1/users, /v2/users) is the most common and visible approach. Clients know which version they're calling; multiple versions can run simultaneously. The downside: clients must update URLs when migrating; old versions must be maintained indefinitely (or until all clients migrate). Deprecation policy: announce deprecation 6–12 months in advance; return Deprecation and Sunset headers on deprecated endpoints to give clients time to migrate.

Header versioning (Accept: application/vnd.company.api.v2+json) keeps URLs clean but requires explicit header management by clients and is harder to test in a browser. GitHub's API uses header-based versioning. Schema versioning (GraphQL deprecation directives @deprecated(reason: 'Use newField instead')) allows granular field-level deprecation within a single schema version—more flexible but requires client tooling to surface deprecation warnings.

Additive changes are always backward compatible: adding optional fields, adding new endpoints, adding new enum values (with caution—existing clients switch to default on unknown values in switch statements). Breaking changes: removing or renaming fields, changing field types, removing endpoints, changing authentication schemes. Run a consumer-driven contract testing tool (Pact) to detect breaking changes before deployment.

deepDive.title: API Gateway Patterns
paragraphs: An API gateway is the single entry point for all API traffic. It handles: authentication (verify JWT before forwarding to services), rate limiting (per-client, per-endpoint), request routing (route /api/v1/users to user-service, /api/v1/orders to order-service), protocol translation (REST->gRPC), response caching, and observability (trace correlation, logging, metrics). AWS API Gateway, Kong, and Envoy Proxy are common implementations.

Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) pattern: instead of a single API gateway, create a dedicated backend for each frontend (web BFF, mobile BFF, IoT BFF). Each BFF aggregates calls to multiple microservices and shapes the response for its specific client's needs. The web BFF returns rich data for a full browser; the mobile BFF returns compact data optimized for bandwidth-constrained devices. This pattern avoids the 'one size fits none' problem of a universal API.

API composition: when a client needs data from multiple services, the API gateway or BFF performs fan-out (call multiple services in parallel) and aggregation (merge results into one response). Service-to-service calls should be direct (gRPC); only final responses aggregated for clients should traverse the gateway. Putting the gateway in the critical path for all inter-service communication creates a bottleneck.

expert.title: Expert: OpenAPI, Contract Testing, and API Governance
paragraphs: OpenAPI (Swagger) specification should be generated from code annotations (not written manually) to stay in sync with implementation. Code-first generation (FastAPI, Go-swagger, Spring Springdoc) produces accurate specs without manual maintenance. The spec enables: automatic SDK generation (OpenAPI Generator produces clients in 30+ languages), interactive API docs (Swagger UI, Redoc), mock server generation for client development before the server is built, and schema validation middleware to automatically validate requests and responses.

API governance at scale (100+ APIs, dozens of teams) requires standards enforcement. API linting tools (Spectral by Stoplight) enforce standards—no 500 without error_id, no unbounded list endpoints, required security schemes—as part of CI/CD. API catalogs (Backstage, SwaggerHub) provide discoverability: developers can find existing APIs before building new ones. Breaking change detection (Optic, Bump.sh) fails CI when a new version introduces breaking changes without a version bump.

examples.title: Stripe's API Design Excellence
examples.description: Stripe's REST API is widely regarded as the gold standard. Idempotency keys on all charge operations prevent duplicate charges during retries. Consistent error codes (card_declined, insufficient_funds) enable programmatic error handling. Versioning via date-based API versions (2024-11-19) lets clients pin to a specific behavior. Pagination uses cursor-based next_page tokens. These design decisions have enabled Stripe to serve millions of developers with minimal support burden.

examples.title: GitHub's GraphQL API
examples.description: GitHub migrated from REST to GraphQL for its v4 API, eliminating the most common complaint about their v3 REST API: too many round trips to assemble a full repository view. A single GraphQL query can fetch repository details, recent commits, open pull requests, and collaborators in one request. The strongly-typed schema serves as living documentation; GraphiQL's autocomplete makes exploration intuitive without reading docs.

keyTakeaways: REST organizes APIs around resources; HTTP verbs express operations; use status codes semantically
GraphQL eliminates over/under-fetching; DataLoader prevents N+1; schema is a breaking-change surface
gRPC + Protobuf is 3–10x faster than REST+JSON; use for internal microservice communication
Idempotency keys make POST operations safely retryable; implement on all mutating endpoints
Cursor-based pagination is stable during insertions/deletions; preferred over offset for user-facing lists
API governance at scale requires linting, contract testing, and a catalog for discoverability
whyItMatters: APIs are the interfaces that allow systems, teams, and products to evolve independently. Poor API design causes cascading problems: clients break on updates, pagination causes memory exhaustion, missing idempotency causes duplicate transactions. Good API design—consistent, evolvable, secure—pays dividends for years. Every system design interview includes API design, and candidates who can reason about resource modeling, error handling, and versioning demonstrate production engineering maturity.
